clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in CACNA1A, which encodes the alpha-1A pore-forming subunit of the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav2.1 that governs presynaptic calcium entry and neurotransmitter release
The gene classically causes episodic ataxia type 2, familial hemiplegic migraine type 1, and spinocerebellar ataxia type 6, but severe variants produce a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
The encephalopathic phenotype features early-onset seizures, which may include epileptic spasms and other refractory types, alongside profound developmental impairment
Cerebellar signs are a recurring theme across the spectrum, with ataxia, nystagmus, and progressive cerebellar atrophy on imaging
Paroxysmal features such as hemiplegic migraine attacks, episodic ataxia, and recurrent episodes of encephalopathy or coma, sometimes triggered by minor head trauma, can occur
Both gain- and loss-of-function mechanisms are recognised across the phenotypic spectrum, influencing whether migraine, ataxia, or epilepsy predominates
Recognising the calcium-channel basis helps frame counselling about the varied paroxysmal neurological features and trauma-triggered episodes
reference.pathophysiology: CACNA1A encodes Cav2.1, the alpha-1A subunit of the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel that is densely expressed at presynaptic terminals and in cerebellar Purkinje cells, where calcium influx triggers neurotransmitter release and shapes network signalling. Different classes of variant produce distinct functional effects: gain-of-function changes enhance calcium entry and are linked to hemiplegic migraine, whereas loss-of-function and expansion mechanisms underlie episodic and progressive ataxia. Severe, often de novo variants disrupt channel function sufficiently to impair cortical and cerebellar development, producing a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with prominent cerebellar involvement. The channel's central role in synaptic transmission accounts for the mixture of epilepsy, ataxia, and paroxysmal phenomena.
additionalDifferentials: SCN1A-related Dravet syndrome and hemiplegic migraine mimics
ATP1A2 and SCN1A familial hemiplegic migraine
Other genetic causes of infantile epileptic spasms
STXBP1 and other developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: Gene panel or whole-exome sequencing, with attention to point variants and CAG repeat expansions in CACNA1A
Electroencephalography to characterise spasms and other seizure types
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to assess cerebellar atrophy and exclude structural causes
Documentation of paroxysmal episodes including migraine and episodic ataxia
Functional or genotype interpretation to gauge gain versus loss of function
redFlags: Trauma-triggered episodes of profound encephalopathy, hemiplegia, or coma
Epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia or refractory status epilepticus
reference.prognosis: The developmental and epileptic encephalopathy phenotype generally carries significant intellectual disability with cerebellar impairment, whereas milder allelic disorders such as episodic ataxia or hemiplegic migraine have far better cognitive outcomes.
pitfalls: Forgetting that CACNA1A causes a wide allelic spectrum beyond episodic ataxia and migraine
Missing trauma-triggered encephalopathic episodes and their risk
Overlooking cerebellar atrophy as a diagnostic clue
Assuming a single functional mechanism across this varied phenotype
references: ILAE resources on calcium-channel developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
management: Control seizures with antiseizure medication tailored to the seizure types, including epileptic spasms and refractory focal seizures.
Treat and prevent episodic ataxia with acetazolamide, and consider aminopyridine for cerebellar symptoms.
Manage hemiplegic migraine with prophylaxis and abortive therapy, avoiding vasoconstrictive triptans and ergot derivatives.
Support development with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy for the associated cerebellar and cognitive impairment.
Recognise and manage trauma-triggered episodes of encephalopathy or coma with supportive intensive care and counsel on avoiding minor head injury.
Monitor for progressive cerebellar atrophy and nystagmus with periodic neurological and imaging review.
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, testing parents to confirm de novo status.
Coordinate care through paediatric neurology and epileptology with multidisciplinary input.
